Name: Pre-Colonial Homelessness
Description: Earliest cases of homelessness are documented in the American colonies.
Source: Community Solutions
Photo: Poor people coming to a workhouse for food, c. 1840

Name: Poorhouses
Description:
first poor house in the colonies opens in New York City -- outside the city wall. 
 Boston and Philadelphia soon follow, opening poor houses of their own -- Boston's Long Island housed homeless folks
Poor houses served as jails, homeless shelters, almshouses, and as de facto mental institutions
Source: Community Solutions
Photo: The first Alms House, 'Poor House'

Name: Native Removal
Description: Indian Removal Act -- first major federal legislation to create mass homelessness
Source: Community Solutions
Photo: Map of Native American Removal from the Southeast

Name: Vagrancy Laws
Description: Boston, New York, Philadelphia during Industrial Revolution shifting rural-urban conditions of housing stability, leading to the development of vagrancy laws. Vagrancy records suggest a rise in the numbers of those in search of work in these cities. Led to the creation of lodging rooms in police stations to hold those with no official, personal residence.
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States
Photo: Phila[delphia] Alms House a busy corner in the shoemaker's room by Alice Barber Stephens

Name: Vagrant, Vagabond
Description: To mean someone who wanders from place to place with no stable home. Vagrancy laws targeted objectionable “out of place” people rather than any particular conduct.
Source: US Vagrancy Laws by Risa L. Goluboff and Adam Sorensen
Photo: A group of vagrants leaves a New York police station in the morning having stayed there overnight to avoid having to sleep on the streets during the winter (1877)

Name: Tramps
Description: men traveling the nation with no visible means of support; used to reference 'an invigorating walking expedition' and during the Civil War 'a long, tiresome walk or march.' . This “army” of overwhelmingly young, able-bodied, white men created a culture that blended the search for work with a love of the open road and a disdain for the constraints of workers in industrialized America.
Source: Citizen Hobo: How a Century of Homelessness Shaped America by Todd DePastino
Photo: Tramps

Name: Hobo
Description: culture of migratory laboring. Understood and depicted in popular culture as an escape from the oppression and monotony of factory work. This culture faded by the 1920s when companies sought loyalty and longeveity of their workforce, and seasonal jobs began to be replaced by cheap immigrant labor.
Source: Jack London on the Road The Tramp Diary and Other Hobo Writings by Richard W. Etulain
Photo: A migrant worker sleeps in a field on bed of straw, hat over his face, barefoot. United Kingdom. Date unspecified.

Name: Urban Slums Study
Description: 1892 Congress allocated $20,000 to the Department of Labor (DOL) to investigate urban slums in cities with at least 200,000 resident
Source: Investigation of the slums of cities. March 10, 1892 H. Rept. 52-625
Photo: Bandit's Roost by Jacob August Riis (1888), depicting the dangerous alley, Bandit's Roost, at 59½ Mulberry Street in New York Citty

Name: Tenement Housing Reform
Description: The effect of tenement housing conditions for the urban immigrant poor led to a social movement of documentation and public recognition of the substandard living conditions that had shaped much of New York City. In 1898 the Tenement House Committee formed leading to the New York State Tenement House Act of 1901. This act was the first law to ban dark, poorly ventilated housing buildings, and created the first set of architectural standards through legal enforcement.
Source: Tenement House Reform in New York, 1834-1900
Photo: Tenement House Department complaint by Harvey T. Warren (1914)

Name: River Displacement
Description: Mississippi River floods displacing hundreds of thousands, creating mass homelessness; President Hoover uses Black men to forcibly rebuild levees
Source: Community Solutions
Photo: "Birdsong Camp at Cleveland, Miss. 4-29-27." Group photograph of flood refugees. Illinois Central Railroad Company

Name: Great Depression
Description: Great Depression creates homelessness and unemployment at never before rates
Source: Community Solutions
Photo: Turpentine worker's family near Cordele, Alabama. Father's wages one dollar a day. This is the standard of living the turpentine trees support by Dorothea Lange

Name: Public Finance for Affordable Housing Production
Description: Emergency Relief and Construction Act of 1932 authorized the Reconstruction Finance Corporation to lend public funds to corporations to build housing for low-income families. National Industrial Recovery Act of 1933, which allowed the Public Works Administration (a government-sponsored work program) to use federal funds for slum clearance, the construction of low-cost housing, and subsistence homesteads; close to 40,000 housing units were produced that year.
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States
Photo: [Apartment building model: P.W.A. Low Rent Housing] by Harris & Ewing (1935 or 1936)

Name: Federal Production of Housing and Urban Improvement
Description: National Industrial Recovery Act of 1933, which allowed the Public Works Administration (a government-sponsored work program) to use federal funds for slum clearance, the construction of low-cost housing, and subsistence homesteads; close to 40,000 housing units were produced that year.
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States
Photo: Barry Farm Dwellings, 1944

Name: Housing Act 1
Description: Housing Act of 1954 continued and broadened slum clearance and urban redevelopment in inner cities
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States
Photo: North End, Corner Hanover and Tileston Streets, 1932 (Boston Public Library).

Name: Housing Act 2
Description: Housing Act of 1956 (P.L. 84-1020) that relocation payments were authorized to those individuals and families who were displaced by the process of urban renewal
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States
Photo: Baltimore’s Abandoned Neighborhoods

Name: Deinstitutionalization Drives Incarceration
Description:
Two major shifts began in the 1960s, ramping up and becoming a norm by the 1990s: major shift : deinstitutionalization of mentally ill w/o adequate and affordable housing = streets / temporary shelters 
major shift : mass incarceration creates a two-way pipeline between homelessness and jails/prisons.
housing discrimination, gentrification, and the disparate impact of local zoning ordinances = puts Black and POC at higher risk of homelessness
Photo: Alcatraz, Military Prison

Name: Robinson v. California
Description: It is unconstitutional for a state to punish a defendant for drug addiction, which is a status rather than an act, when the defendant has not engaged in any illegal conduct involving drugs in the state.
Source: Robinson v. California
Photo: Massachusetts War on Drugs Photo Archive, 1960s–1980s

Name: Housing and Urban Renewal Act
Description: The Housing and Urban Renewal Act of 1965 (P.L. 89-117) was enacted as a rent supplement for low-income, disabled, and elderly individuals. Legislation in 1965 also formally created the Department of Housing and Urban Development
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States
Photo: CORE-sponsored demonstration at realtor office of Picture Floor Plans, Inc.

Name: Powell v. Texas
Description:
Police arrested Leroy Powell for public intoxication. He was tried, convicted, and fined $20 in the Corporation Court of Austin Texas.
Powell argued that criminal punishment for public intoxication is cruel and unusual punishment in violation of the Eighth Amendment, because he had chronic alcoholism. 
He appeared in public drunk as a compulsive symptom of the disease, not his own choice. The County court of Travis County held that alcoholism is not a defense to the charge and affirmed the conviction.
Source: Powell v Texas
Photo: Chronic inebriates such as the one pictured here may become victims of crime as they are less capable of defending and caring for themselves.

Name: Fair Housing Act
Description: Finally, Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, the Fair Housing Act, established fair housing provisions to prohibit discrimination in access to housing.
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States
Photo: Mass protests in support of the Fair Housing Act

Name: Public Funding Reduction
Description: 80% reduction in federal investments in public housing + cuts to social safety = massive spike in homelessness
Source: Community Solutions
Photo: Homeless in LA

Name: Housed
Description: Individuals living in single room occupancy hotels (SROs) and other (flophouses, cheap hotels, and temporary housing) were legally defined by HUD as housed, and not homeless, making the studying of homelessness hard to identify. Post-WWII the shift from white male homelessness was due to the increase of the poorest, disabled, verteran, and welfare dependent individuals into these forms of housing insecurity, while not being considered homeless.
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States
Photo: An Overlooked Solution to the Affordable Housing Crisis: Hotels

Name: Housing and Community Development Act of 1974
Description: The Housing and Community Development Act of 1974 (P.L. 97-35) merged several urban development programs into the broader Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) program. This law created the Housing Choice Voucher program, also known as the Section 8 program, to provide low-income housing through rental subsidies paid to the private sector.
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States
Photo: President Gerald R. Ford signs into law the Housing and Community Development Act of 1974

Name: Federal Homeless Definition
Description:
The Stewart B McKinney Homeless Assistance Act defined homelessness as: (1) Individuals and families who lack a fixed, regular, and adequate nighttime residence and includes a subset for an individual who is exiting an institution where he or she resided for 90 days or less and who resided in an emergency shelter or a place not meant for human habitation immediately before entering that institution;

(2)
Individuals and families who will imminently lose their primary nighttime residence;

(3)
Unaccompanied youth and families with children and youth who are defined as homeless under other federal statutes who do not otherwise qualify as homeless under this definition; or

(4)
Individuals and families who are fleeing, or are attempting to flee, domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, stalking, or other dangerous or life-threatening conditions that relate to violence against the individual or a family member. The McKinney Act also created a targeted Health Care for the Homeless (HCH) primary care funding stream, with a distinct broad definition of homelessness, which now exists within the Federally Qualified Health Center (FQHC) program.
Source: Community Solutions
Photo: History of the McKinney-Vento Act

Name: Callahan v. Carey
Description: paved the way for further legal victories that ensured the right to shelter for homeless men, women, children, and families in New York City.
Source: Callahan v. Carey
Photo: Shelters save lives

Name: Urban Shifts and AIDS
Description: Some main causes of homelessness at this time include: gentrification of the inner city, deinstitutionalization of the mentally ill, high unemployment rate, the emergence of HIV/AIDS, an inadequate supply of affordable housing options, and deep budget cuts to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and social service agencies in response to what was then the country's worst recession since the Great Depression; this all coincided with:  rapid increase of property value in downtowns ; elimination of SROs and rooming houses for apartments + condominimums
Source: Community Solutions
Photo: Homeless in LA

Name: Social Security Amendments Act of 1980
Description: President Carter signed the Social Security Amendments of 1980. Chief changes: a more stringent maximum family benefit calculation; greater work incentives for disabled Social Security and SSI beneficiaries; and increased authority given the Secretary of HHS to establish, through regulations, performance standards and administrative procedures to be met by the States, including the authority to overturn State disability determination decisions.
Source: Social Security Chronology
Photo: Community Care - Fighting the Cuts

Name: Cuts to Social Service
Description: This era of tighter public spending and cuts to social programs, including: tightening of the disability eligibility process (Social Security Act of 1980);  impeding efforts of disabled and ill to receive financial benefits (Social Security Disability Benefits Reform Act of 1984).
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States
Photo: Aug. 14, 1935, file photo President Franklin Roosevelt signs the Social Security bill in Washington

Name: Criminalization of Public Space
Description:
This era represented the introduction of ordinances criminalizing life-sustaining acts such as selfsheltering (“camping”), sleeping, resting, eating, or asking for donations
ordinances for  jaywalking or littering, to harass and push homeless persons out of certain spaces.
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States
Photo: Homelessness in the street

Name: Increased Public Commitment to Affordable Housing
Description: Affirms the national goal that every American family should be able to afford a decent home in a suitable environment. States that the objective of national housing policy shall be to reaffirm the long-established national commitment to decent, safe, and sanitary housing by strengthening a nationwide partnership of public and private institutions capable of carrying out such policy.
Source: Cranston-Gonzalez National Affordable Housing Act
Photo: Secretary Turner meeting with the Manufactured Housing Association for Regulatory Reform

Name: AIDS and homelessness
Description: The co-currence of AIDS and homelessness led to the creation of the Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS (HOPWA) program through the Cranston-Gonzalez National Affordable Housing Act.
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States
Photo: Diagnosed with HIV in 1993, Mr. E. says more rent relief would make his life easier.

Name: Literal Homelessness
Description: Shift in social science to describe those with no access to conventional dwellings, such as houses, apartments, mobile homes, rooming houses, or SROs.
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States
Photo: Homeless on the street of Los Angeles

Name: Interagency Council on Homelessness
Description: The 1997 Stewart B. McKinney Act also authorized the creation of the U.S. Interagency Council on Homelessness (USICH). USICH is an independent executive branch body established to better coordinate homelessness programs across government agencies. The USICH includes representative membership from all major federal agencies whose mission touches upon homelessness, including, among others, HHS, HUD, the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA).1
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States
Photo: HHS Secretary Becerra leads the USICH meeting

Name: Quantification of Homelessness
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States
Photo: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions, by Thomas Kuhn

Name: Collaborative Approaches
Description:
Federal, national, and local initiatives to address homelessness begin to adopt shared frameworks
and best practices in preventing to and responding to homelessness
Source: Community Solutions
Photo: On August 14, 2025, Skid Row celebrated the Grand Opening of the Skid Row Care Campus

Name: Chronic Homelessness Initiative
Description: Chronic Homelessness Initiative, asking states and local jurisdictions to create 10-year plans to end chronic homelessness. Another change in federal policy occurred in 2003, bringing a focus on “ending chronic homelessness” through low-threshold and permanent supportive housing programs
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States

Name: HEARTH Act
Description:
Reauthorization of the McKinney-Vento Act, called the HEARTH Act	
	The reauthorization consolidated several existing programs for individuals experiencing homelessness, created a federal goal that individuals and families experiencing homelessness be permanently housed within 30 days, and codified the planning processes used by communities to organize into Continuums of Care in order to apply for homeless assistance funding through 
	New definitions of “homeless,” “homeless person,” and “homeless individual” were expanded. These changes were based on Congress identifying (1) a lack of affordable housing and limited housing assistance programs, and (2) an assertion that homelessness is an issue that affects every communit
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States
Photo: Obama Signs Heinrich Bill To Boost Tribal Home Ownership

Name: City Encampments
Description: laws in 187 cities and found that city-wide bans on camping have increased by 92%, on sitting or lying by 78%, on loitering by 103%, on panhandling by 103%, and on living in vehicles by 213%
Source: The History of Homelessness in the United States

Name: Federal Strategic Plan to End Homelessness
Description: Opening Doors:  the first-ever comprehensive federal strategic plan to prevent and end homelessness. The plan set the stage for HUD’s goals of preventing and ending homelessness for veterans by 2015; preventing and ending homelessness for individuals experiencing chronic homelessness by 2017; preventing and ending homelessness for families, youth, and children by 2020; and ultimately setting a path to ending all types of homelessness.
Source: End Homelessness

Name: Decriminalizing Homelessness
Description: Three key solutions: The creation of comprehensive and seamless systems of care. Collaboration between law enforcement, behavioral health, and social service providers. Alternative justice system strategies.
Source: Searching out Solutions: Constructive Alternatives to the Criminalization of Homelessness

Name: Addressing Encampent
Description: This report is designed to assist communities in developing an action plan that will link people experiencing homelessness and living in an encampment, with permanent housing opportunities.
Source: Ending Homelessness for People Living in Encampments: Advancing the Dialogue

Name: Norton v. City of Springfield
Description:
The ordinance defines panhandling as an oral request for an immediate donation of money. Signs requesting money are allowed, as are oral pleas to send money later
The Seventh Circuit upheld the ordinance in 2014, but granted rehearing in light of the Supreme Court’s 2015 decision, Reed v. Gilbert, and reversed.
Source: Norton v. City of Springfield, No. 13-3581

Name: Bell v. City Boise
Description:
a case brought by homeless plaintiffs who were convicted under Boise ordinances that criminalize sleeping or camping in public.
Statement of Interest of DoJ: allege that enforcement of the city of Boise ordinances prohibiting sleeping or camping in public outdoor places, on nights when there is insufficient shelter space in Boise to accommodate the homeless population, amounts to cruel and unusual punishment in violation of the Eighth Amendment
Source: Bell v. City of Boise

Name: Guidance on Youth Homelessness
Description: This report is designed to assist communities in developing an action plan that will link people experiencing homelessness and living in an encampment, with permanent housing opportunities.
Source: Dept of Education issues guidance for homeless youth

Name: Martin v Boise
Description: in the 9th Circuit, successfully defended from Supreme Court review in 2019, which held that in the absence of adequate alternatives, it is cruel and unusual punishment under the 8th Amendment to punish someone for life-sustaining activities like sleeping, resting, or sheltering oneself.
Source: Martin v. Boise

Name: Second Strategy to End Homelessness
Description: Trump Era plan to end homelessness
Source: The Federal Strategic Plan to Prevent and End Homelessness

Name: Anti-Criminalization
Description: EO 13929, promoted use of law enforcement to force individuals into mega-tent shelters, though the Administration continued promoting increased law enforcement approaches behind the scenes; George Gloyd Law Enforcement Act, anti-criminalization provisions.
Source: Executive Order 13929

Name: Whole-of-Government Response
Description: Expanding the Toolbox: The Whole-of-Government Response to Homelessness, envisions an approach that dramatically reduces homelessness by engaging and assessing families and individuals with a trauma-informed approach to care that addresses the real root causes of homelessness.
Source: Expanding the Toolbox

Name: Housing First
Description: House America is a national partnership in which HUD and USICH invite mayors, county leaders, Tribal nation leaders, and governors to use the historic investments provided through the American Rescue Plan to address the crisis of homelessness through a Housing First approach by immediately re-housing and building additional housing for people experiencing homelessness.
Source: USICH, HUD Launch House America Initiative to Address Homelessness Crisis

Name: Housing is a Human Right Act
Description: the bill establishes additional taxes on: (1) the sale or exchange of real property if the amount realized from the transaction is at least $10 million, (2) the sale or exchange of real property involving an anonymous entity, and (3) rent received by landlords that own large amounts of dwelling units.
Source: H.R.1708 - Housing Is a Human Right Act of 2023

Name: The Ending Homelessness Act of 2023 (H.R. 4232)
Description: Would transform the Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) program into a federal entitlement, meaning every eligible household would receive assistance.
Source: The Ending Homelessness Act of 2023

Name: Housing Crisis Response Act of 2023 (H.R. 4233)
Description: The official page on Congress.gov for the bill, which would provide over $150 billion in investments for public housing, affordable housing production, and rental assistance.
Source: Housing Crisis Response Act of 2023

Name: Coalition on Homelessness v. City and County of San Francisco
Description: Litigation challenging San Francisco's practice of towing and selling vehicles used as shelter by unhoused residents for unpaid parking tickets, arguing it violates California's constitutional protection of property rights and due process.
Source: Coalition on Homelessness v. City and County of San Francisco

Name: Disability Rights California v. Newsom (Regarding the CARE Act)
Description: Challenges to California's Community Assistance, Recovery, and Empowerment (CARE) Act on due process grounds, arguing it creates a coercive treatment system without mandating housing, which fails to adequately address unsheltered homelessness.
Source: drc-v-newsom

Name: Johnson v. Grants Pass
Description: The enforcement of generally applicable laws regulating camping on public property does not constitute “cruel and unusual punishment” prohibited by the Eighth Amendment.
Source: Johnson v. Grants Pass

Name: Byrd v. State of Missouri (Regarding anti-camping laws)
Description: Challenges to a Missouri law that codified a model anti-camping ordinance, arguing it was passed unconstitutionally by violating the state's "single subject" rule, which illegally restricted local authority to address homelessness.
Source: missouri/supreme-court
